abstract: A technical solution, bilateral V-Y advanced flaps,was used to repair the upper lip defect. The flaps work very well for patients with a depth of #5 mm defects covering one-third to one-half of the upper lip without involving the philtral ridge. One V-shaped flap was designed at the oral vestibule adjacent to the defect and another at the cutaneous side. The skin incision along the markings was made down to the subcutaneous tissue and the cutaneous flap was mobilized toward the adjacent mucocutaneous junction. Then, the mucosal flap was elevated onto the superficial layer of the orbicularis muscle, thereby creating a blood supply based on the vascular plexus formed by the small branches of the superior labial artery and the orbicularis muscle. To ensure refined vermiliocutaneous match, the inferior margins of the flaps were fixed with the base of the vermilion border using a 5-0 absorbable suture. Finally, we used a 6-0 suture to close the defect after trimming the excess skin around it (Fig 2). The flaps, which avoid microstomia and irregularity in vermilion, are highly recommended.

Before beginning the procedure on the scalp, the lesion border is demarcated with a skin marker, and a 2-cm circular margin is drawn for a running locking hemostatic suture placement. Subsequently, the lesion and perilesional zone is injected with 1% lidocaine and epinephrine. Once appropriately anesthetized, a larger size suture, such as a 3-0 or 4-0 prolene running locking hemostatic suture, is placed at the 2-cm boundary to effectively occlude the small blood vessels and provide appropriate hemostasis prior to excision (Figs 1 and 2). After properly anchoring the suture, the excisional process begins while ensuring negative margins. The use of electrocautery is not required during the procedure. Subsequently, a running subcuticular purse string technique with an absorbable suture, such as a 4-0 vicryl, is placed to decrease the size of the wound bed. After the procedure, the wound is adequately dressed and follow-up is scheduled. This novel combined suture technique described for non-melanoma skin cancer scalp excisions aims to improve hemostasis and decrease the use of electrocautery. This method reduces intraoperative time and potential scarring from overuse of electrocautery. To properly validate this new surgical technique and integrate its benefit into current practice, further studies are required. Use of similar suture hemostatic techniques have been described in plastic surgery literature, such as during pediatric cranioplasty, wherein minimizing blood loss and transfusion is paramount.1 We hope the readers can add this technique to their armamentarium to use in instances when electrocautery is not available, such as low resource health care settings.

CLINICAL CHALLENGE Deroofing is an in -office technique for hidradenitis suppurativa that is typically locally curative for the specific lesion treated. It is a superior option over incision and drainage, due to lower recurrence rates (100% for incision and drainage vs 4%-19% for deroofing), minimal complications, and high patient satisfaction. 1 Conventional deroofing typically entails administering local anesthesia, removing the roof of each abscess/ tunnel and exposing all interconnected cavities using scalpel, scissors, electrosurgery, or a CO 2 laser. 2 Punch debridement, also called mini-deroofing, is a simpler technique suitable for managing small abscesses or tunnels and requiring the same skillset as a punch biopsy. 2 However, many providers remain unaware of this treatment option and the technique. SOLUTION Here, we provide a simple video demonstrating the punch debridement technique and required tools for the treatment of hidradenitis suppurativa (Video 1, available on www.jaad.org). Following local anesthesia, a 5 -to8 -mm circular disposable biopsy punch is used to access the cavity and release any drainage. Then, a curettage or grattage, using gauze wrapped around a cotton swab, is utilized to debride the cavity lining. Hemostasis is accomplished with aluminum chloride. Healing occurs by secondary intention, and wound care with petrolatum and bandages is typically recommended for 4 to 8 weeks. While the recurrence rate following punch debridement has not been studied specifically, it is likely similar to deroofing, making it a simple and effective technique. This procedure's simplicity allows for easy adaptation from dermatology or primary care clinics to the emergency department, with the potential to supplant incision and drainage with a more effective procedure.

Pachyonychia congenita is a group of rare keratinization disorders primarily characterized by the triad of palmoplantar keratoderma, nail hypertrophy, and plantar pain (Figs 1-8).1 Estimated prevalence is 5000 to 10,000 patients worldwide, though true prevalence is likely higher due to underdiagnosis of milder subtypes.2 Plantar pain is often debilitating and significantly affects quality of life.3,4 Most cases are inherited in an autosomal dominant fashion, though around 30% are due to de novo mutations.3 There are 5 types of pachyonychia congenita caused by mutations in keratin genes KRT6A, KRT6B, KRT6C, KRT16, and KRT17.1
